title: Design Tic-Tac-Toe / a Generic Board Game (OOD)
prompt: Design Tic-Tac-Toe, then generalize it toward an N x N board (Connect-style) game. Model the Board, Player, Move, and Game classes, the turn/state flow, and the win-detection logic. Make the win check efficient rather than scanning the whole board every move. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: A small board game done cleanly — legal-move validation, an efficient incremental win check, and a design that generalizes to N x N.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Clarifies board size (3x3 vs NxN), number of players/symbols, win condition (full line vs K-in-a-row), and human-vs-AI before designing.

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Identifies Board, Cell, Player, Piece/Symbol, Move, and Game/GameController.

rubric.label: Class design
rubric.description: Board owns the grid and validation, Player holds a symbol, Move is a value object; no god-class Game holding raw arrays.

rubric.label: Win detection
rubric.description: Efficient incremental win check (row/col/diag counters updated per move, O(1)) rather than O(N^2) full scan each turn.

rubric.label: State machine
rubric.description: Clear game state flow: IN_PROGRESS -> WIN / DRAW, turn alternation, and rejecting moves after game over.

rubric.label: Relationships
rubric.description: Game aggregates Players and composes a Board; Board composes Cells; correct ownership/multiplicity.

rubric.label: API methods
rubric.description: makeMove(player, row, col), isValidMove, currentPlayer, getStatus/getWinner; clean signatures.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: Generalizes to NxN / K-in-a-row / more players, and to an AI player, without rewriting the core.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Occupied cell, out-of-bounds move, move out of turn, move after game over, full-board draw.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains the incremental win check clearly and reasons about the NxN generalization.

functional_requirements: Two players alternate placing their symbol on an N x N board
Validate each move (in bounds, cell empty, correct player's turn, game not over)
Detect a win (a full line for 3x3; K-in-a-row for the general case) and a draw
Report current player, game status, and winner
Generalize from 3x3 to N x N and optionally to an AI opponent
nonfunctional_requirements: Win detection efficient — ideally O(1) per move, not O(N^2)
Clean separation of board mechanics, rules, and game orchestration
Extensible to larger boards, K-in-a-row, and more players / AI
clarifying_questions: Fixed 3x3 or general N x N? Is the win condition a full line or K-in-a-row?
Two players only, or more symbols?
Human vs human, or do we need an AI player?
Do we need move history / undo?

core_classes.name: Game / GameController
core_classes.responsibility: Orchestrates the match: whose turn, applies moves via the board, checks status, ends the game.
key_methods: GameStatus makeMove(Player p, int row, int col)

core_classes.name: Board
core_classes.responsibility: Owns the grid and move validation; applies a piece and delegates/holds incremental win-check counters.
key_fields: int[] rowCount, colCount; int diag, antiDiag (per symbol)
key_methods: boolean place(Piece piece, int r, int c)
boolean isWinningMove(Piece piece, int r, int c)

core_classes.name: Cell
core_classes.responsibility: One grid position; empty or holding a Piece (can be modeled implicitly by the grid array).

core_classes.name: Player
core_classes.responsibility: A participant bound to a Piece/symbol; may be human or AI.

core_classes.name: Move
core_classes.responsibility: Immutable value object: which player placed which piece where.

core_classes.name: PlayerStrategy (interface, optional)
core_classes.responsibility: Human input vs AI move selection (minimax), pluggable.

relationships: Game composes a Board and aggregates Players (2..*)
Board composes Cells / owns a Piece grid and the win-check counters
Player has-a Piece and optionally a PlayerStrategy (human vs AI)
Move associates a Player with a board position (value object)

design_patterns.where: PlayerStrategy for human vs AI (minimax) move selection
design_patterns.why: Add an AI opponent without changing the game loop.

design_patterns.where: GameStatus governing whether moves are accepted

design_patterns.why: Vary board setup without caller knowledge.

apis: GameStatus makeMove(Player p, int row, int col)
state_transitions: IN_PROGRESS --winning move--> WIN (game over, reject further moves)
IN_PROGRESS --valid move, no win--> IN_PROGRESS (advance to next player)
edge_cases: Cell already occupied — reject the move
Move played out of turn — reject / enforce currentPlayer
Move after game is over — reject
Full board with no winner — declare DRAW
K-in-a-row on a large board — win line may not touch an edge
concurrency: Turn-based and effectively single-threaded; note that a networked multiplayer version serializes moves per game and validates the mover is currentPlayer
If moves arrive concurrently, guard makeMove so only one move mutates the board at a time
extensibility: N x N and K-in-a-row: parameterize Board with size and k; win counters generalize
More players/symbols: Piece enum + per-symbol counters
AI opponent: a PlayerStrategy (minimax/alpha-beta) — game loop unchanged
Undo/replay: keep a move history stack
Other line games (Connect Four): reuse Board/win-check with a gravity rule on placement

deep_dives.probe: Scanning the whole board every move is O(N^2). How do you check for a win in O(1) using per-row/col/diagonal counters, and how do you extend that to K-in-a-row?
What changes moving from fixed 3x3 to N x N with K-in-a-row? Which classes stay untouched?
How would you add an unbeatable AI without touching the game loop — where does minimax live?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions scan or loop or check all
followup_bank.question: Checking every row/col/diagonal each move is O(N^2). Can you keep counters per line and detect a win in O(1) per move?
Now generalize to N x N with K-in-a-row — what changes, and which classes stay the same?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions ai or bot or computer
followup_bank.question: Where does the AI live so the game loop doesn't change — a PlayerStrategy with minimax?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions array or grid in game
followup_bank.question: Should the raw grid live in Game or in a Board class? Why does that separation matter?

tradeoffs: Incremental counters (O(1) check, more state to maintain) vs full scan (simple, O(N^2))
Cell objects (explicit, flexible) vs a plain Piece[][] grid (compact, fast) — grid is usually enough
Template/Strategy generalization (reusable across line games) vs a tight 3x3-only design (simpler now)
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer separates Board (owns the grid, validation, and win state) from Game/GameController (turn order, status) rather than piling raw arrays into one class. Players bind to a Piece enum; Move is an immutable value object. The standout is win detection: instead of an O(N^2) scan each turn, maintain per-row, per-column, and two diagonal counters per symbol updated on each placement, giving an O(1) win check, and generalize it to K-in-a-row for the N x N case. Game status is a small state machine that rejects moves after WIN/DRAW and detects the full-board draw. The candidate handles occupied/out-of-bounds/out-of-turn/after-over edge cases, and shows the design generalizes to N x N, more players, and an AI opponent via a PlayerStrategy (minimax) without touching the game loop.

interviewer_notes: Junior-level, but the discriminator is the win check — many candidates scan the whole board every move. Let them, then ask for O(1): per-line counters updated on each placement. If they get that, push the K-in-a-row generalization (counters no longer suffice for arbitrary K on a large board — segment counting along the placed line is the next step; reward candidates who notice). Insist the raw grid lives in a Board class, not the Game god-object. Check that moves are rejected after game over and that draw is detected. Don't demand an AI or heavy patterns from a junior; forcing minimax or a rules engine onto tic-tac-toe is the over-engineering trap. If time remains, ask where an AI would plug in (PlayerStrategy) to confirm the loop stays closed.
